assessment.note: Same PMQ source states 25 lb/person/year and about 46 slices/person/year; internally consistent at ~1.84 slices/lb, but both are old (page dated 2015) and likely based on industry lore rather than a measured survey.

Both from the same 2024 Pizza Hut/Talker Research press release: 288 slices/person/year and 95 billion slices nationwide. 95e9 / 288 ≈ 330M people, consistent with US population, but they are not independent measurements.

The '100 acres/day' and '350 slices/second' figures recur across PMQ (2015), Economic Times (2025) and Prepared Foods (2023); they are the same industry meme copied across outlets, not independent evidence. 350 slices/s ≈ 30.2M slices/day ≈ 11 slices/person/year, far below the 46–288 slices/person/year figures, so the meme is internally inconsistent with per-capita claims.

Per-capita pizza consumption estimates range from 23–25 lb/year (p4, p25) to 46 slices/year (p5), 156 slices/year (p145, Gozney survey of pizza lovers), and 288 slices/year (p10, Pizza Hut press release). The 288 figure implies ~156 lb/person/year, implausible against total US cheese consumption (~40 lb/person/year), so p10/p11 are likely inflated or refer to a different concept (e.g., slices sold including frozen, or a marketing exaggeration).

USDA/NHANES 2017–2020: 11% of the population consumes pizza on any given day; males average 4 slices and females 3 slices per eating occasion. These are the most methodologically credible inputs for a frequency-based decomposition (d4).

Economic Times (2025): 3 billion pizzas/year excluding frozen, 4 billion including frozen. At ~8 slices/pizza this implies 24–32 billion slices/year, or ~73–97 slices/person/year, bracketing the PMQ 46-slice and Gozney 156-slice estimates but well below the 288-slice claim.

Chicago pizza restaurant counts differ by source and definition: RentechDigital reports 1,987 pizza restaurants in Chicago (April 2026), while Foodeist's indexed sample lists 283. The Rentech figure is likely a broad establishment count (including chains, takeout, etc.); Foodeist is a curated sample. Both are kept but used with different roles.

ListWithClever reports Chicago has 6.0 pizza restaurants per 100,000 residents vs a national average of 12.4 — i.e., Chicago under-indexes on pizza restaurant density. This conflicts with Chicago's reputation as a pizza city and with the 1986 survey (p201) naming Chicago the biggest pizza fans. The density metric may reflect Chicago's high population density and large restaurant market rather than per-capita pizza consumption.

1986 Chicago Tribune survey: Chicagoans averaged 34.8 pizza meals/year vs Los Angeles <20. This is old but is the only direct evidence that Chicago over-indexes on pizza frequency relative to other cities.

2002–2003 Consumer Expenditure Survey: Chicago CMSA households spent more on food away from home ($2,583 vs $2,243 US) and total food ($6,001 vs $5,357), suggesting a local propensity to spend more on food, which could support a modest positive Chicago adjustment.
ListWithClever Pizza Passion Score: Chicago 83.1 vs national 68.3 (search-interest based), indicating higher pizza engagement in Chicago.

Slice platform data: top-quartile pizzerias average $658,548 annual sales (median $561,278). These are for top-quartile clients, not average pizzerias, so they represent an upper bound on per-store revenue.
Papa Johns 2024 10-K: domestic company-owned units average $1.3M/year, North America franchised units average $1.1M/year. These are chain averages and can anchor per-store sales for chain pizzerias.

Chain store density in Illinois: Domino's 1.8 per 100k (US avg 1.9), Pizza Hut 1.3, Papa John's 0.7. Illinois is close to the national average for chain pizza density, suggesting no strong chain-driven over- or under-supply.

extra_directions.hypothesis: A recent (2020s) survey of Chicago residents' pizza eating frequency and slices per occasion would directly anchor the frequency route (d4) and resolve the conflict between the 46-slice and 288-slice national estimates. Currently the only Chicago-specific frequency evidence is from 1986 (p201), which is too old to transfer without a large adjustment.
extra_directions.data_to_find: Survey data on how often Chicago adults eat pizza (times per month) and average slices per occasion, ideally from a local university, market research firm, or city health department.

extra_directions.hypothesis: A direct estimate of annual pizza sales in Chicago (city or metro) would enable the bottom-up sales route (d2) without relying on national per-capita figures. Currently we have only national pizza sales (p164) and Chicago deep-dish niche revenue (p50), which is too narrow.
extra_directions.data_to_find: Annual pizza restaurant sales for the City of Chicago or Chicago MSA, from sources like Technomic, NPD Group, or the Illinois Restaurant Association.

extra_directions.perspective: Slices per whole pizza in Chicago
extra_directions.hypothesis: The conversion from whole pizzas to slices is a key uncertainty. Chicago-style deep-dish and thin-crust pizzas may have different slice counts than the national average of 8. A local estimate of slices per pizza would improve all routes that convert between pies and slices.
extra_directions.data_to_find: Average number of slices per pizza sold in Chicago, by style (deep-dish, thin-crust, stuffed). Could come from pizzeria menus, industry reports, or local surveys.

params.formula: p137 * mean(p138, p139) * a1 * 2700000 * k_days_per_year

p137.role: Share of US population consuming pizza on any given day (NHANES 2017-2020), used as base daily frequency for Chicago

p138.role: Average slices consumed by males at an eating occasion (US, NHANES), used in mean with p139

p139.role: Average slices consumed by females at an eating occasion (US, NHANES), used in mean with p138

a1.role: Chicago pizza consumption index relative to US average (dimensionless)

methods.rationale: Frequency-based decomposition (d4): daily eating probability (p137) times average slices per occasion (mean of p138 and p139) times Chicago population (2.7M) times a Chicago adjustment factor (a1). This yields slices per day. The NHANES data are the most methodologically sound inputs for pizza consumption frequency. The Chicago index a1 adjusts for local over/under-indexing. Uncertainty in a1 and in the NHANES estimates (which are national, not Chicago-specific) is propagated via Monte Carlo. Failure mode: NHANES may undercount pizza consumption if respondents underreport; the Chicago index is uncertain.

params.formula: p79 * p95 / p37 * a2 * a3 / k_days_per_year

p79.role: Number of pizza restaurants in Chicago (establishment count, 2026)

p95.role: Average annual sales per pizzeria (top quartile of Slice clients, used as proxy for average Chicago pizzeria revenue)

p37.role: Average listed pizza price in Chicago (USD per pizza item)

a3.role: Share of pizza consumption from restaurants vs grocery/frozen (scaling factor to total consumption)

methods.rationale: Bottom-up sales-based route (d2): number of Chicago pizza restaurants (p79) times average annual sales per restaurant (p95, top-quartile Slice data used as a proxy for average Chicago pizzeria revenue) divided by average price per pizza (p37) gives pizzas sold per year. Multiply by slices per pizza (a2) and scale by share of consumption from restaurants (a3) to account for grocery/frozen pizza, then divide by days per year. This route is independent of per-capita surveys. Failure modes: p95 is for top-quartile Slice clients, likely higher than average Chicago pizzerias; p37 is an average menu price, not necessarily the price per whole pizza; a3 is uncertain.

params.formula: p10 * 2700000 * a1 / k_days_per_year

p10.role: US average pizza consumption per person per year in slices (2024, PMQ/Pizza Hut)

a1.role: Chicago pizza consumption index relative to US average (dimensionless)

methods.rationale: National per-capita baseline (d1): US per-capita pizza consumption of 288 slices/year (p10) times Chicago population (2.7M) times a Chicago adjustment factor (a1), divided by days per year. This route uses the most recent national per-capita figure but is highly uncertain because p10 (288 slices) is much higher than other estimates (46, 156) and may be inflated. The Chicago index a1 adjusts for local differences. Failure mode: p10 may be a marketing exaggeration; if true per-capita is lower, this method overestimates.

assumptions.name: Chicago pizza consumption index relative to US average
assumptions.rationale: Chicago is widely regarded as a top pizza city. The 1986 survey (p201) showed Chicagoans ate 34.8 pizza meals/year vs Los Angeles <20, suggesting an over-index. The ListWithClever Pizza Passion Score (p220 vs p221) shows Chicago at 83.1 vs national 68.3, a ratio of 1.22. However, restaurant density (p218 vs p219) shows Chicago at 6.0 vs national 12.4, suggesting under-indexing on supply. We balance these signals and set the index at 1.15 with a wide range (0.9–1.5) to reflect uncertainty. This factor is applied to the national per-capita rate to get a Chicago-specific rate.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to adjust a national per-capita pizza consumption rate to Chicago. Assumes Chicago's relative pizza consumption is stable and can be approximated by a combination of survey and search-interest evidence.
assumptions.falsified_by: A direct Chicago-specific consumption survey showing per-capita pizza intake at or below the national average, or evidence that Chicago's pizza culture is primarily tourist-driven rather than resident-driven.

assumptions.name: Slices per whole pizza
assumptions.rationale: Standard large pizzas are typically cut into 8 slices. Chicago deep-dish pizzas are often cut into 6–8 slices, while thin-crust may be cut into 8–12. The midpoint of 8 is a reasonable central value with a range of 6–10 to cover style variation.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert whole pizzas to slices in any route that estimates pizza consumption in pies.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that Chicago pizzerias systematically cut pizzas into a different number of slices (e.g., a local survey showing average slices per pizza is 6 or 10).

assumptions.name: Share of pizza consumption from restaurants vs grocery/frozen
assumptions.rationale: NHANES (p143) states 'Over half of pizza was obtained from restaurants and one quarter was obtained from the grocery store', implying roughly 75% from restaurants/food service and 25% from grocery (including frozen). This assumption is used to scale restaurant-based estimates to total pizza consumption. The range reflects uncertainty in the exact split.
assumptions.applies_when: Used when a method estimates only restaurant pizza sales and needs to be scaled to total pizza consumption including frozen/prepared at home.
assumptions.falsified_by: A recent survey showing a significantly different split between restaurant and grocery pizza acquisition in Chicago.

assumptions.name: Average slices per pizza order
assumptions.rationale: An average pizza order may include multiple slices or a whole pizza. Given that a whole pizza is ~8 slices and orders often feed 2–3 people, 2.5 slices per order is a reasonable central estimate. This is used to convert order counts to slice counts in the sales-based route.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in the sales-based route (m2) to convert number of orders to slices.
assumptions.falsified_by: Data showing average pizza order size in Chicago is significantly different (e.g., average order is a whole pizza per person).

assessment.note: Same PMQ sentence: 25 lb/person/year and ~46 slices/person/year are two expressions of one measurement, not independent. Implies ~1.84 slices/lb, i.e. a heavy slice (~245 g) — inconsistent with typical 100-150 g slices, so the 46-slice figure is internally suspect.

Same 2024 PMQ/Pizza Hut page: 288 slices/person/year and 95 billion slices nationwide. 95e9/288 ≈ 330M people, so these are one internally consistent arithmetic pair, not two sources. 288 slices/year ≈ 0.79 slices/person/day, roughly 6x the 46-slice figure.

National per-capita pizza rates span 46 to 288 slices/person/year (6x). The 350 slices/second figures (p29, p162) imply ~11 billion slices/year ≈ 33/person/year, a third distinct level. These are marketing-statistic aggregates of unknown method; they cannot be reconciled and must be treated as a wide prior, not a point value.
23 lb (2025) vs 25 lb (2015) per-capita pizza consumption — mutually consistent on the weight basis and suggest mild decline; both are secondary citations of industry statistics.

3B non-frozen + 1B frozen = 4B pizzas/year; same source, consistent decomposition. With ~330M people this is ~12 pizzas/person/year, i.e. ~1 pizza/month, which is a useful independent anchor on pies rather than slices.

Single USDA/NHANES source: 11% of population eats pizza on a given day; 4 slices (male) / 3 slices (female) per occasion. Internally consistent and the most methodologically credible frequency evidence, but US-wide and 2017-2020 vintage.

NHANES-implied rate (0.11 × ~3.5 slices/day ≈ 0.39 slices/person/day ≈ 140/year) sits between the 46 and 288 figures and near the Gozney 156/year survey. The 288 figure is an outlier against every other route.
Survey-based slices/year (156) and ~3 slices per sitting are consistent with the NHANES frequency route; all are self-reported consumption surveys, so they share social-desirability and recall bias.

Per-store annual sales cluster: Slice top-quartile $561k-$659k, Papa Johns $1.1-1.3M, Domino's $1.37M, Pizza Hut $0.82M, Little Caesars $1.17M, segment AUV $1.01M. Chain AUVs are higher than the Slice indie top quartile, so using p95 for all Chicago pizzerias likely understates revenue per store.

Illinois chain store density: Domino's 1.8 vs US 1.9 per 100k, Pizza Hut 1.3, Papa Johns 0.7. Illinois is at or slightly below national chain density — argues against a large Chicago over-index on chain pizza volume.

1986 survey: Chicago 34.8 pizza meals/year vs LA <20. Establishes Chicago as a high-frequency market historically, but 40 years old; usable only as a directional prior on the local index, not a level.

US pizza sales $56B (2022) vs chain-segment sales implied by units × AUV (~$33B LSR pizza + FSR) — different scopes (all pizza vs top-500 chains) but same order of magnitude; supports using revenue routes with a chain/indie split.
Restaurant-industry output for Chicago MSA ($46.99B) and Illinois by segment — a denominator for a pizza share of restaurant sales, but no pizza share is supplied, so this route needs an assumption.

Cheese consumption: 39.5-39.9 lb/person/year total, mozzarella 12.5 lb. Mozzarella is the pizza-relevant flow, but the pizza share of mozzarella is unknown, so the physical-flow route (d5) cannot be closed without an extra coefficient.

assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that frozen/homemade pizza accounts for more than ~40% of Chicago pizza occasions.

assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that non-pizzeria outlets sell a large share (>30%) of Chicago restaurant pizza.

assumptions.falsified_by: Data showing frozen pizza below 10% or above 40% of US pizza volume.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
